content: Oxidative stress is considered a significant factor in the development of pre-eclampsia. It has been hypothesized that providing antioxidant supplements to pregnant women may mitigate oxidative stress, potentially preventing or delaying the onset of pre-eclampsia. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of antioxidant supplementation during pregnancy in reducing the risk of pre-eclampsia and its associated complications. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of May 2007), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (up to Issue 3, 2006), MEDLINE (from 1950 to October 2007), and Current Contents (from 1998 to August 2004). The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials that compared one or more antioxidants with either a placebo or no antioxidants during pregnancy for the prevention of pre-eclampsia. Trials comparing different antioxidants or antioxidants with other interventions were also included. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated their quality, and extracted the relevant data. The review included ten trials involving a total of 6,533 pregnant women. Five of these trials were considered to be of high quality. In most of the trials, the antioxidant intervention consisted of combined vitamin C and vitamin E supplementation. The analysis revealed no statistically significant difference between the antioxidant and control groups in terms of the relative risk of developing pre-eclampsia (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.06; nine trials, 5,446 women). Similarly, there was no significant difference in other primary outcomes, including severe pre-eclampsia (RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.76; two trials, 2,495 women), preterm birth before 37 weeks of gestation (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.22; five trials, 5,198 women), small-for-gestational-age infants (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.11; five trials, 5,271 babies), or neonatal death (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.53; four trials, 5,144 babies). However, women who received antioxidant supplementation were more likely to report abdominal pain in late pregnancy (RR 1.61, 95% CI 1.11 to 2.34; one trial, 1,745 women). They were also more likely to require antihypertensive therapy (RR 1.77, 95% CI 1.22 to 2.57; two trials, 4,272 women) and antenatal hospital admission for hypertension (RR 1.54, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.39; one trial, 1,877 women). Despite these findings, there was no clear evidence of an increase in other hypertensive complications. The authors concluded that the evidence from this review does not support the routine use of antioxidant supplementation during pregnancy to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia or other serious pregnancy-related complications.
